title: Why Haven't Trump's Tariffs Crashed the Economy?
summary: Economist answers audience questions on the hot September 2026 CPI: why inflation feels worse than measured, PPI pressure, and why tariffs added modestly to inflation but still lower living standards.

assertions.quote: I believe the truth is the cost of living for the typical American rose by 3.7% over the past year.

verdicts.note: The CPI is the consensus measure built from hundreds of thousands of price quotes; known biases are small relative to the gap between measured and perceived inflation.

assertions.quote: the method for calculating the consumer price index did not change

verdicts.note: The 2026 methodological tweaks were to the BEA's PCE deflator, scheduled in advance; the BLS CPI series was unchanged.

assertions.quote: there's good evidence that people's perceptions of the state of the economy and the cost of living rise and fall with gas prices

verdicts.note: Survey research consistently finds inflation perceptions track gasoline and grocery prices and show loss aversion and telescoping bias.

assertions.quote: We also discover a lot of that is that we buy gasoline. And if you strip out food and energy, we're back down to 2.6%.
if your input costs are rising, then that's going to lead to price rises. So inflation will start to move towards the PPI.

verdicts.note: PPI leads CPI only loosely and pass-through is partial, but sustained input-cost inflation above consumer inflation does compress margins until prices adjust.

A 10 percent duty on imported inputs raises producer prices in consumer goods industries by about 2.6 percent, and a 10 percent tariff-induced rise in pre-retail prices raises retail prices by 5.6 percent, consistent with full pass-through net of distribution margins, with the input-cost channel taking nine to twelve months.

assertions.quote: Inflation has roughly speaking been 1 to 2% higher than it would otherwise have been.

verdicts.note: Fed and academic estimates put the 2025 tariffs' contribution at roughly one to two points on the price level spread over a year or more, not the surge some predicted.

assertions.quote: the United States is a remarkably closed economy which is to say relative to other countries very little of what we buy is imported

verdicts.note: Imports are roughly a tenth of US consumer spending, so even high tariffs move the overall price level by only a few percent.

The direct effect scales with the imported share of each good and a uniform 10 percent tariff raises consumer goods prices only 2.6 percent, but a third of that effect comes through domestically produced goods via imported inputs and markups, so a low import share limits the effect less than the direct channel alone would suggest.

assertions.quote: you sort of wouldn't raise your prices until it was completely clear what was going on. And so, that would slow down the rate

verdicts.note: Retail pass-through in 2025 was gradual and incomplete, consistent with firms waiting, but price trackers also saw some sellers raise prices as soon as tariffs were announced.

Firms told the NY Fed surveys that uncertainty over future tariff rates, exemptions and retaliation may be leading them to adopt cautious, incremental pricing rather than large discrete adjustments, extending the pass-through period.

assertions.quote: So now what happens is prices rise and wages don't rise. That's the economics of a supply shock.

verdicts.note: Tariffs do reduce real incomes as a cost-push shock, but protected domestic producers gain revenue and nominal wages are not literally frozen.

assertions.quote: if it all happened at once, inflation would be 2 to 4% higher. It may not all happen at once.
Paychecks are also falling behind, so people are able to buy less with what they have.
